account: Researchers at the University of Stirling's Institute of Aquaculture applied Observe's algorithm to feed-camera video at two commercial Atlantic salmon marine farms in Scotland. Three of the six authors work at Observe Technologies, which is based in Richmond, United Kingdom, so the paper is the developer's own evidence. Innovate UK funded the study in partnership with Observe and AKVA Group. The algorithm, a patented convolutional neural network (EP3644717), ran on video in every cage, with 5 and 4 extra cameras in one cage per farm. It outputs “activity” (%), which combines fish abundance, speed and shoal cohesion. Two Stirling observers found that the algorithm's activity output tracked their own fish counts on 55 video stills (R² of 0.70). Gill health, operational welfare indicators, mortality and specific feeding rate were scored weekly. Data were collected from 10 May to 10 September 2023 at Farm A and from 22 June to 13 October 2023 at Farm B. Gill health problems arose at both farms in summer 2023. Mean activity in the two months before was 25.6 ± 10.5% (A) and 24.9 ± 7.0% (B). It rose for two months after to 43.6 ± 15.1% and 32.6 ± 9.6%, with fish moving to the cage center. In a mixed model, the authors found that proliferative gill disease was the main driver. In the paper, published on 15 August 2025, they propose behavior as a non-invasive welfare indicator. They report no alert that preceded diagnosis and no change in treatment.

ai_role.statement: The vendor's neural network turned feed-camera video into an activity measure, and two Stirling observers checked that measure against their own fish counts on 55 video stills (R² of 0.70). Farm staff identified the gill disease by weekly scoring. The study shows that activity rose with the disease and does not show that the signal came first or changed a decision.

system: Observe Technologies behavioral monitoring algorithm (patented convolutional neural network, EP3644717)
title: Observe Technologies' camera AI registers behavioral change when gill disease hits two Scottish salmon farms
unrated_because: The study reports a correlation between the activity signal and gill disease, and the authors report no diagnosis, treatment or welfare outcome that the signal changed.
